voce: It claims better reasoning and coding while cutting down the time and length of its answers.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is the latest release from DeepSeek. According to the model card it contains 763.2 billion parameters, but only 228.1 billion are active for each token thanks to a mixture‑of‑experts design. The context window stretches to one million tokens, far beyond most open models. All the weights are released under an MIT license, so you can download them from Hugging Face and run them yourself if you have the hardware.

This version is a minor update over DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, but the model card says it delivers substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks. It also reduces the time it takes to finish a task and the length of the generated output, which means lower compute cost. Those changes push the performance‑cost trade‑off forward for many agent‑style applications.

The DeepSeek team reports a range of benchmark numbers. On the HLE without tools test the model scores 42.6, up from 36.8 in the previous version. Terminal‑Bench 4.0 rises to 42.3 from 31.2. ProgramBench, which measures coding ability, goes to 29.1 compared with 20.3 before. In the visual BabyVision benchmark with tools, it reaches 92.5, beating its predecessor’s 89.6. These figures suggest consistent gains across several domains.

According to the card, the model shines in reasoning, coding, and visual tasks, and it runs faster with shorter replies. The one‑million token context is a clear advantage for long‑form work. However, the memory demand is huge – at 4‑bit precision it still needs about 465 GB for an 8K context, and no home machine on our list can hold it fully. So while the capabilities are impressive, the hardware requirement is a major limitation.

If you are a researcher who needs a massive context window, or a developer building autonomous agents that benefit from better reasoning and coding, this model could be a good fit. It’s also suitable for anyone who wants free, open weights and is ready to handle the memory demands. For hobbyists without high‑end hardware, the size may be prohibitive, but the MIT license means you can experiment on cloud resources if you prefer.
What do you need to run it at home? At 4-bit it takes about 465 gigabytes of memory. No single home machine on our list holds it fully.
There is no free API for it yet. The weights are open: you can download them from Hugging Face under the MIT license. Arena has not ranked it yet: we add the score as soon as the votes arrive.
